# The Predictive Power of Earnings Surprises in a Monthly Stock Panel

## Abstract

We evaluate ten firm characteristics as predictors of next-month stock returns in a balanced panel of 500 index constituents over 120 months. Among the candidates, only standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) exhibits a statistically and economically significant cross-sectional relationship with future returns, with a mean monthly rank IC of 0.0998 and a t-statistic of 23.25. A quintile long-short portfolio based on SUE yields an average monthly return of 3.04% and an annualized Sharpe ratio of 7.31. All other characteristics show negligible or statistically insignificant predictive power after accounting for the panel structure.

## Methods

We use a monthly panel of 60,000 stock-month observations (500 stocks × 120 months). The universe is point-in-time: each month includes the 500 stocks that were index constituents at that time, and stocks later removed (e.g., due to distress or delisting) remain in the data up to their removal month, including the final-month return.

We analyze ten candidate features: book_to_market, gross_prof, log_mktcap, asset_growth, accruals, sue, idio_vol, leverage, turnover, and rd_intensity. For each feature, we compute the monthly rank (Spearman) correlation with next-month returns (`ret_next`) across the 500 stocks, then average these monthly rank ICs over the 120 months. We report the mean rank IC, its standard deviation, an associated t-statistic (mean / std × sqrt(120)), the proportion of months with positive IC, and the performance of an equal-weighted long-short portfolio that buys the top quintile and sells the bottom quintile of the feature each month.

A feature is considered a valid signal if (i) its rank IC t-statistic exceeds 2.0 in absolute value, (ii) its sign is consistent with economic priors or has a plausible mechanism, and (iii) its long-short portfolio has a meaningful Sharpe ratio. Features that fail these criteria are rejected.

## Results

The table below summarizes the signal statistics for all ten features.

| Feature | Mean Rank IC | IC t-stat | Long-Short Monthly Return | Long-Short Annualized Sharpe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| book_to_market | -0.0030 | -0.72 | -0.11% | -0.27 |
| gross_prof | 0.0039 | 0.93 | 0.10% | 0.26 |
| log_mktcap | 0.0001 | 0.02 | 0.03% | 0.08 |
| asset_growth | 0.0061 | 1.64 | 0.28% | 0.72 |
| accruals | 0.0055 | 1.34 | 0.29% | 0.70 |
| **sue** | **0.0998** | **23.25** | **3.04%** | **7.31** |
| idio_vol | 0.0043 | 1.14 | 0.03% | 0.08 |
| leverage | -0.0043 | -1.00 | -0.02% | -0.05 |
| turnover | 0.0001 | 0.02 | 0.01% | 0.02 |
| rd_intensity | -0.0002 | -0.05 | 0.05% | 0.13 |

Only SUE passes our validity thresholds. Its mean rank IC of 0.0998 is more than an order of magnitude larger than any other feature, with a t-statistic of 23.25—overwhelmingly significant. The sign is positive: stocks with higher standardized unexpected earnings tend to have higher next-month returns. The long-short quintile portfolio earns 3.04% per month on average, with an annualized Sharpe of 7.31. The proportion of months with positive IC is 99%, indicating remarkable consistency.

All other features have rank IC t-statistics below 2.0 in absolute value and long-short Sharpe ratios below 0.75. Their mean rank ICs are close to zero, and none shows a reliable directional tilt across months.

## Discussion

The dominance of SUE is consistent with the post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) literature: standardized unexpected earnings capture the market's short-term underreaction to earnings news, leading to predictable drift in subsequent months. The point-in-time construction of SUE—using the most recent fiscal quarter ending on or before the end of month t and consensus forecasts available at that time—avoids look-ahead bias and makes the signal implementable in real time.

The lack of predictive power for other characteristics is notable. Value (book_to_market), profitability (gross_prof), size (log_mktcap), investment (asset_growth), accruals, idiosyncratic volatility, leverage, turnover, and R&D intensity all show economically negligible and statistically insignificant rank ICs in this sample. This may reflect the specific index universe (large, liquid constituents), the relatively short 10-year sample, or the fact that these characteristics are already priced in by the market within this universe.

The proposed trading strategy is straightforward: at the end of each month, rank all 500 stocks by SUE, buy the top quintile (100 stocks) and sell the bottom quintile (100 stocks) in equal weights, holding for one month. Given the observed long-short monthly return of 3.04% and the monthly standard deviation implied by the Sharpe ratio (3.04% / (7.31 / sqrt(12)) ≈ 1.44%), the expected annualized return is approximately 36.5% (before costs) with an annualized Sharpe of 7.31. However, these figures are gross of transaction costs and may be inflated by the small universe size and the specific sample period.

## Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, the sample covers only 120 months and 500 stocks per month, all drawn from a single broad equity index; results may not generalize to other markets or time periods. Second, the reported long-short returns are gross of transaction costs, which could be substantial for a monthly-rebalanced strategy with 200 positions. Third, the SUE signal may be subject to data-snooping bias, as it is the only strong signal among ten candidates; its true out-of-sample performance may be lower. Fourth, the point-in-time universe construction, while realistic, may still contain survivorship or selection effects that influence the results. Finally, the analysis does not account for risk factors beyond the long-short construction; the high Sharpe ratio may reflect exposure to systematic risks not captured here.
